extractions.source_title: Understanding and Managing Black Rot Disease in Coffee - Agriculture Notes

disease_name.evidence: Black rot disease is one of the most destructive fungal diseases affecting coffee plantations

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Black rot is caused by the fungus Koleroga noxia (also referred to as Corticium koleroga or Pellicularia koleroga in older literature)

type_of_disease.evidence: Black rot disease is one of the most destructive fungal diseases affecting coffee plantations

affected_parts.evidence: attacks all aerial parts of the coffee plant — leaves, twigs, branches, and berries — but not the roots

summary.value: Dark spots on leaves that enlarge and turn jet black, with dark brown or black decaying leaves, twigs, and berries. White web-like fungal threads hold dead plant parts in place on branches.
summary.evidence: Small dark spots form on leaf surfaces — usually near the margins or along the midrib where water tends to collect. These spots enlarge rapidly and turn jet black, giving the disease its common name.

diagnostic_features.value: White, web-like fungal threads (mycelium) visible on twigs and petioles that hold dead leaves and berries attached to branches instead of falling. Sclerotia (resting bodies) scattered over affected areas.
diagnostic_features.evidence: White, web-like fungal threads become visible on twigs and petioles, holding leaves and berries in place even after they die. This is a key identifying feature: dead leaves do not fall freely but remain attached to branches, suspended by the mycelial threads of the fungus. Sclerotia (resting bodies of the fungus) can also be seen scattered over affected areas.

Coffee Leaf Miner | Pests & Diseases - Plantix

affected_parts.evidence: irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface. Appearance of pale yellow trails under coffee leaf epidermis. Presence of large necrotic patches. ... Plants become defoliated and eventually die off.

summary.value: Irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface, pale yellow trails under the leaf epidermis, and large necrotic patches caused by larval mining of the mesophyll.
summary.evidence: Occurrence of irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface. Appearance of pale yellow trails under coffee leaf epidermis. Presence of large necrotic patches.

diagnostic_features.value: Mines formed by larvae visible as pale yellow trails under the leaf epidermis, developing into large necrotic patches; larvae transparent and up to 3.5 mm in length found within mines; silk X-shaped cocoons in the axial region of the leaf.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Initially, mines are formed and later develop over a large surface area leading to large necrotic patches. The larvae are present in the mines and feed on the mesophyll. ... the larvae leave the lower side of the eggs that are in contact with the upper leaf epidermis and get into the leaves. The larvae are transparent and reach 3.5 mm in length. ... Larvae leave the mines and weave a silk X-shaped cocoon, usually in the axial region of the leaf
